description.narrative: Sexual exploitation of children (SEC) is a grave violation of children’s rights and affects millions of children and youth annually, regardless of gender. No region, country or child is immune, though girls, boys and children with other gender identities face differing levels of risk to different manifestations of SEC depending on their intersectional vulnerability factors. It impacts heavily and long lastingly on their physical, emotional and mental well-being. It deprives children and youth of establishing healthy (sexual) relationships and from developing to the best of their potential. The SUFASEC programme is designed to combat SEC and will work in 12 countries in Latin America and South and South East Asia: Bangladesh, Bolivia, Brazil, Colombia, Dominican Republic, Guatemala, India, Indonesia, Laos, Nepal, Philippines and Thailand.

The SUFASEC programme is designed to combat SEC by working towards the following long-term impact: “Children in all of their diversity are better protected from sexual exploitation.” This activity forms part of the SUFASEC programme. The long-term impact will be reached through three interlinking objectives that address different dimensions (social norms, assets/environments, and laws/policies/systems). 1. Children, youth and their communities successfully challenge social norms and harmful practices related to SEC 2. Children and youth have access to and are supported by strengthened assets and protective environments 3. Children and civil society meaningfully participate in holding duty bearers, including government and local authorities, accountable to their obligations towards improved (implementation of) laws, policies, and systems

The different stakeholder groups involved in the SUFASEC programme include: - Children and youth in all their diversity: A child-centred approach: children and youth are the most important stakeholders. When children/youth fall victim to SEC the physical and mental impact can be long lasting. The Alliance adheres to the UN definition of child (0-18 years) and youth (15-24 years) - Caregivers and Communities: Critical stakeholders in the community include parents, caregivers, community leaders, teachers, local Community Based Organisations (CBOs), social workers, and other community members involved in community based child protection mechanisms. - CSOs and CBOs: Local child protection organisations support and implement activities at community level, L&A towards national actors, and provide synergies of interventions. - Local and national governments: formulate, endorse and implement laws and public policies related to SEC - Private Sector: Travel and tourism orgs (e.g., large and small, hotels, transport), as well as ICT/ Digital Service Providers have interest to avoid SEC taking place within their value chain, and to avoid having their products and services used to facilitate SEC - International donors, Intergovernmental bodies, INGOs, Multilateral entities55: Targeted audiences and partners for evidence based regional and international lobbying - Dutch Stakeholders: NL Embassies in programme countries, MoFA, MoJ&S, to formalise the network for sustainable cooperation to end SEC and impunity of offenders. The Dutch Public - Media & Journalists: Investigative and reporting outlets in the Programme countries. Media and journalists in the Netherlands.

title.narrative: Children and youth access comprehensive correct SRHR and SEC information
# of young people (male) reached with comprehensive, correct information on sexuality, HIV/AIDS, STIs, pregnancy and contraception

comment.narrative: Since we are looking at people reached with information given by SUFASEC during programme, we set this baseline value as zero

The group is composed by adolescents between 14 and 17 years old, enrolled in the public education system, who will be provided with information on SEC off and online, GBV and SRHR. The SRHR theme will serve as an intersectional perspective, guiding work with diverse population groups, The group includes children indigenous origin such as the Wayus, Venezuelan migrants, Afro-descendants and Colombian returnees. This approach will help young boys understand how SEC violates their rights and affects their sexual development, empowering them to question and challenge the social constructs that have historically justified violence against boys..

We have worked with 5 young boys between 14 and 16 years old.They received training in SEC and SEC online, GBV and SRHR The SRHR theme is a cross-cutting perspective that guides the work with different population groups such as young people or communities. Opening the debate on SEC under this approach allows for other readings, other perspectives and the analysis of other risks that directly or indirectly affect SEC. Children's understanding and recognition of their SRHR also implies that they are able to identify how SE violates and violates them, directly affecting their sexual development under conditions of autonomy and integrity. The aim is for them to demystify from their own realities those social imaginaries that have historically justified violence in the bodies of girls, boys and women. .

title.narrative: Greater and safer access to quality child protection and local SRHR information and services

comment.narrative: Since we are looking at people reached with information given by SUFASEC during programme, we set this baseline value as zero

The population that will receive care in the partner's shelter home will be composed of young survivors of SEC, aged between 13 and 16 years old. This population will include Colombian (including returnees), Venezuelan, Afro-descendant and indigenous girls from the cities of Cartagena and La Guajira. Access to services will be provided in partnership with public and private institutions, as part of the process of restitution of victims' rights.

We worked with 2 young male survivors of CSEC, between 13 and 14 years old, who have accessed DSDR services and say they feel safe. It is important to consider that they are in a process of restitution of rights and have access to comprehensive care at home, with food, schooling, health, housing, therapeutic care and the possibility of developing a life project. Their training includes various topics, including STIs, which are also the result of the commodification and instrumentalisation of sexuality. Therefore, at the time of accessing services, they are more empowered in their SRHR.

# of women led CSOs with increased L&A capacities

comment.narrative: Since we are studying the people to whom the information provided by SUFASEC reaches during the program, we set this reference value at zero

DTZ partner Fundación Renacer is an NGO with more than 30 years of experience in the fight against CSEC. It has three lines of action (Research, Intervention and Prevention) that constitute a comprehensive programme to tackle the crime. It provides care through two homes in Cartagena and La Guajira and prevention projects in 8 other departments where advocacy is crucial. In this sense, it promotes dialogues with intersectoral roundtables, articulating mechanisms and committees to fight against human trafficking and CSEC. It also has experience in promoting advocacy at regional, departmental, municipal and national levels with representatives and decision-makers in the legislative and public policy spheres. It also promotes the direct action of youth groups such as EICYAC, community leaders with a defined ethnic approach and institutional agreements for the design and implementation of synergistic actions to not only mitigate the negative impacts of CSEC but also to prevent them. In this sense, the desired future capacity is: to have more tools and instruments for social and political advocacy, to strengthen the synergic response to cases of CSEC and to consolidate protective environments that provide a strong and robust prevention strategy.-
